usamts-2016-r2-01.title: Aim for 2 shaded cells per line
usamts-2016-r2-01.body:
Every row and every column must contain the same shaded area $s$, so the total shaded area is $11s$, and it may be at most $\frac{121}{2}$; hence $1 \le s \le 5$. Small regions (single cells, dominoes) are the most flexible, so aim for $s = 2$ using small regions.

The official solution shades 12 regions: four single cells, five dominoes and three L-shaped/bent triominoes, $22$ cells in total ($\blacksquare$ = shaded):
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \blacksquare & \blacksquare & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0}\\\hline \phantom{0} & \blacksquare & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \blacksquare & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0}\\\hline \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \blacksquare & \blacksquare & \phantom{0}\\\hline \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \blacksquare & \blacksquare & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0}\\\hline \blacksquare & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \blacksquare & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0}\\\hline \blacksquare & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \blacksquare & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0}\\\hline \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \blacksquare & \blacksquare & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0}\\\hline \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \blacksquare & \blacksquare & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0}\\\hline \phantom{0} & \blacksquare & \blacksquare & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0}\\\hline \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \blacksquare & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \blacksquare\\\hline \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \blacksquare & \blacksquare\\\hline\end{array}$$

Shaded cells by row (columns): row 1: 4, 5; row 2: 2, 7; row 3: 9, 10; row 4: 8, 9; row 5: 1, 6; row 6: 1, 6; row 7: 4, 5; row 8: 7, 8; row 9: 2, 3; row 10: 3, 11; row 11: 10, 11.

**Check.** Each row has 2 shaded cells, and so does each column (column 1: rows 5, 6; column 2: rows 2, 9; column 3: rows 9, 10; column 4: rows 1, 7; column 5: rows 1, 7; column 6: rows 5, 6; column 7: rows 2, 8; column 8: rows 4, 8; column 9: rows 3, 4; column 10: rows 3, 11; column 11: rows 10, 11). Every shaded cell belongs to a region all of whose cells are shaded (checked against the region boundaries in the figure), and $22 \le 60.5$.

**Answer: the shading above.**

usamts-2016-r2-02.title: Eliminate y
usamts-2016-r2-02.body:
Arithmetic progression: $y = \frac{x+z}{2}$. Geometric progression: $y^2 = x(z + 1000)$. Hence
$$\frac{(x+z)^2}{4} = xz + 1000x \iff x^2 + 2xz + z^2 = 4xz + 4000x \iff (z - x)^2 = 4000x.$$

Since $4000 = 400\cdot 10$, we get $10x = \left(\frac{z-x}{20}\right)^2$. A rational number whose square is an integer is an integer, so $10x = k^2$ for an integer $k$; then $10 \mid k^2$ forces $10 \mid k$, say $k = 10n$, so $x = 10n^2$ and $z - x = 20k = 200n$, i.e.
$$x = 10n^2,\quad z = 10n^2 + 200n,\quad y = 10n^2 + 100n.$$

$x \ge 100$ needs $n \ge 4$ ($n = 3$ gives $90$). $z \le 999$ needs $n \le 4$ ($n = 5$ gives $z = 1250$). So $n = 4$: $(x, y, z) = (160, 560, 960)$.

Check: $160, 560, 960$ has common difference 400, and $160, 560, 1960$ has common ratio $3.5$.

**Answer: $(160, 560, 960)$**

usamts-2016-r2-03.title: Construction plus a Bezout shift
usamts-2016-r2-03.body:
Measure positions on the circle as numbers mod 1 (one full turn = 1 = $360^\circ$). The $m$-gon's vertices are $a + \frac im$ and the $n$-gon's vertices are $b + \frac jn$ (all mod 1). We claim the largest possible minimum distance is $\frac{1}{2mn}$ of a turn, i.e. $\frac{360^\circ}{2mn} = \frac{180^\circ}{mn}$.

**Construction.** Take $a = 0$, $b = \frac{1}{2mn}$. Every $m$-gon vertex $\frac im = \frac{in}{mn}$ is an integer multiple of $\frac{1}{mn}$, and every $n$-gon vertex $\frac{1}{2mn} + \frac{jm}{mn}$ is a half-odd-integer multiple of $\frac1{mn}$. Any two such numbers differ (even mod 1) by at least $\frac{1}{2mn}$.

**Upper bound.** Let $d$ be the minimum distance, attained by vertices $x$ (of the $m$-gon) and $y$ (of the $n$-gon) with $x - y \equiv d$ (after possibly reflecting the whole picture, which swaps the sign). Since $\gcd(m, n) = 1$, Bezout gives integers $p, q$ with $pm - qn = 1$. Then $x + \frac qm$ is also an $m$-gon vertex, $y + \frac pn$ is an $n$-gon vertex, and
$$\Big(x + \frac qm\Big) - \Big(y + \frac pn\Big) = d + \frac{qn - pm}{mn} = d - \frac{1}{mn}.$$
So $\left|d - \frac1{mn}\right|$ (taken mod 1) is also a distance between vertices of the two polygons, hence $d \le \left|d - \frac{1}{mn}\right|$. Since $0 \le d$, this forces $d \le \frac{1}{2mn}$ (if $d > \frac1{2mn}$ then $\left|d - \frac1{mn}\right| < d$).

Converting to degrees, the maximum is $\frac{360^\circ}{2mn} = \frac{180^\circ}{mn}$. ∎

**Answer: $\dfrac{180^\circ}{mn}$**

usamts-2016-r2-03.title: Union of the two vertex sets
usamts-2016-r2-03.body:
Rotate so that an $m$-gon vertex is at $0$. The $m$-gon vertices are the multiples of $\frac{1}{m}$ and, since $\gcd(m,n)=1$, the differences $\frac jn - \frac im = \frac{jm - in}{mn}$ run over **all** multiples of $\frac{1}{mn}$ (mod 1). So if the $n$-gon starts at $b$, the set of signed distances from $n$-gon vertices to $m$-gon vertices is exactly $b + \frac{k}{mn}$, $k \in \mathbb Z$ (mod 1). The smallest absolute value in this set is the distance from $b$ to the nearest multiple of $\frac{1}{mn}$, which is at most $\frac{1}{2mn}$, with equality when $b$ is halfway between two multiples. Hence $d_{\max} = \frac{1}{2mn}$ of a turn $= \frac{180^\circ}{mn}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{180^\circ}{mn}$**

usamts-2016-r2-04.title: Counting bound and a flag-bit scheme
usamts-2016-r2-04.body:
**Lower bound.** On a given damaged sheet only $n - 10$ squares are free, so the sender can produce at most $2^{n-10}$ different colorings. To distinguish all $2^{2016}$ messages we need $n - 10 \ge 2016$, i.e. $n \ge 2026$.

**A scheme for $n = 2026$.** Number the squares $1, \dots, 2026$ and split them into 10 classes by residue mod 10. Ten consecutive squares contain exactly one square of each class, so each class contains **exactly one** damaged square. The classes have sizes $k_1, \dots, k_{10}$ with $\sum k_i = 2026$; we show how to send $k - 1$ bits with a class of $k$ squares of which one (unknown in advance to the receiver) is damaged. Then the 10 classes together carry $2026 - 10 = 2016$ bits.

Within a class, call the first square the *flag* and the other $k-1$ squares the *data*. **Decoding:** read the data squares; if the flag is red take them as they are, if the flag is green flip every colour.

**Encoding** of a desired word $w$ of length $k - 1$:
* If the damaged square is the flag: if it is red, write $w$ in the data squares; if green, write $w$ flipped.
* If the damaged square is a data square: if its colour already agrees with the corresponding letter of $w$, colour the flag red and write $w$; otherwise colour the flag green and write $w$ flipped (then the damaged square agrees with flipped $w$ automatically).

In every case the decoder recovers $w$. So $n = 2026$ works.

**Answer: 2026**

usamts-2016-r2-05.title: Pair the sequence with itself
usamts-2016-r2-05.body:
**Step 1: $y_k$ is a quadratic in $k$.** Choose $a, b, c$ with $f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c$ satisfying $f(1) = y_1$, $f(2) = y_2$, $f(3) = y_3$ (possible: a quadratic through three points with distinct $x$-coordinates always exists, by Lagrange interpolation). Every quadratic satisfies $f(k+3) - 3f(k+2) + 3f(k+1) - f(k) = 0$ (it is the third finite difference, which vanishes for polynomials of degree $\le 2$). The recurrence determines $y_4, y_5, \dots$ from the three previous terms, so by induction $y_k = f(k)$ for all $k = 1, \dots, n$.

**Step 2: all $y_k$ vanish.** The hypotheses say $\sum_k y_k k^j = 0$ for $j = 0, 1, 2$; by linearity $\sum_k y_k\, g(k) = 0$ for every polynomial $g$ of degree at most 2. Take $g = f$:
$$\sum_{k=1}^n y_k^2 = \sum_{k=1}^n y_k f(k) = 0.$$
A sum of squares of reals is zero only if every term is zero, so $y_1 = \dots = y_n = 0$, and in particular $\sum k^3 y_k = 0$. ∎

usamts-2016-r2-05.title: Linear system and determinant (official approach)
usamts-2016-r2-05.body:
As in Step 1 write $y_k = ak^2 + bk + c$, and let $p_m = \sum_{k=1}^n k^m$. The three conditions become
$$\begin{aligned} a p_2 + b p_1 + c p_0 &= 0,\\ a p_3 + b p_2 + c p_1 &= 0,\\ a p_4 + b p_3 + c p_2 &= 0. \end{aligned}$$
Using $p_0 = n$, $p_1 = \frac{n(n+1)}2$, $p_2 = \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}6$, $p_3 = \frac{n^2(n+1)^2}4$, $p_4 = \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)(3n^2+3n-1)}{30}$, the determinant of the coefficient matrix simplifies to
$$\frac{1}{2160}\, n^3 (n+1)^2 (n-1)^2 (4 - n^2),$$
which is negative for $n \ge 4$ (e.g. $-80$ for $n = 4$, $-700$ for $n = 5$). So the only solution is $a = b = c = 0$, every $y_k = 0$, and $\sum k^3 y_k = 0$. ∎
